=== cap-flight-01 | Milestone 1: the rules, the status codes and a ring buffer
--- teach
You have written allocators in Systems Programming, schedulers in Operating Systems and hash maps in Data Structures in C++. In this capstone you put that knowledge to work on one program: the core of a spacecraft's flight software. By the last milestone it samples sensors, filters them, checks limits, runs on a fixed schedule, takes commands from the ground, sends telemetry packets down with checksums, notices its own faults and falls back to a safe mode. At the end you fly it for a simulated hour while the checks break things on purpose.

This first lesson sets the rules every line must follow, fixes the project's error codes, and builds the first container, a **ring buffer**.

### The project, milestone by milestone

| # | Milestone | What it adds |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rules, status codes, ring buffer | a fixed-capacity queue |
| 2 | Pool | fixed blocks handed out by handle; packet queues |
| 3 | Static map | a hash map with a fixed number of slots |
| 4 | Bytes and CRC | big-endian reading and writing; CRC-16 |
| 5 | Packet encoder | CCSDS-style headers packed into bits |
| 6 | Decoder | rejecting bad packets; finding packets in a noisy stream |
| 7 | Sensors | calibration and filters, in whole numbers |
| 8 | Limits | limit checks with persistence; stuck sensors; events |
| 9 | Cyclic executive | frames, rate-monotonic order, overruns |
| 10 | Commands | parsing, validating and acknowledging commands; modes |
| 11 | Fault management | detection, isolation, recovery, safe mode |
| 12 | Health and status | the housekeeping report; the downlink |
| 13 | The flight system | every part wired together |
| 14 | A simulated hour | faults injected from a script, responses checked |

Each milestone's starter is the whole project so far, plus empty versions (**stubs**) of the new parts. You fill the stubs in. The checks test the new parts, and they also re-run the key tests of every earlier milestone, so a change that breaks old code is caught at once.

### The four rules

Flight software runs for years with nobody able to press reset. Teams such as NASA's JPL write it under strict rules, like the [[Power of Ten|pot-capstone]]. This project follows four of them.

1. **No heap allocation after start-up.** Every object gets its memory once, at the start, from static arrays and fixed-size pools. The heap can [[fragment|fragmentation]] after days of running, until a request fails even though enough bytes are free in total. And the time `new` takes depends on the heap's history, so you cannot promise it finishes in time. With fixed memory, a program that starts is a program that has all the memory it will ever use.
2. **No exceptions.** The build uses `-fno-exceptions`. An exception is a hidden jump out of any function that calls anything, and a reviewer cannot see where control goes. Every failure here is a value the caller must look at.
3. **No recursion.** Each recursive call takes more stack, and the depth depends on the data. Without recursion the deepest stack can be worked out before launch. Every loop also has a fixed upper bound.
4. **Every function checks its inputs and returns a status code.** A null pointer or an out-of-range number is refused with a code, never trusted.

A **status code** is a value a function returns to say whether it worked and, if not, why. Everyday picture: the little lights on a router. Green, or a colour that tells you which thing went wrong.

### One list of codes for the whole project

There are three common ways to report errors without exceptions:

- **A plain `int`**, like C's `errno` values. Nothing stops you comparing it with the wrong constant, or mixing it up with a count.
- **One enum per module.** Each module is tidy, but every layer has to translate its neighbour's codes, and the translations lose information.
- **One `enum class` for the whole project.** One vocabulary, checked by the compiler.

This project takes the third. The starter gives you the list, all 20 codes, in the order they must keep. It is `enum class Status : std::uint8_t`. The `: std::uint8_t` says each code is stored in exactly one byte, because in milestone 10 the codes travel to the ground inside acknowledgement packets. That is also why the list is never reordered: the ground reads the numbers.

An `enum class` does not turn into an `int` by itself, so `Status::Full == 3` does not compile. You name the code, or cast on purpose:

```cpp fragment
Status s = Status::Full;
if (s != Status::Ok) { /* handle it */ }
int wire = static_cast<int>(s);   // 3: the number that goes into a packet
```

For logs, people need words, not numbers. `status_name` turns a code into its name in capitals. A `switch` over an `enum class` with a `case` for every value lets the compiler warn you when someone adds a code and forgets its name. After the `switch`, return `"UNKNOWN"`, because a byte from a corrupted packet can hold a number that is not in the list at all.

### The heap watch

How can a check prove that your code never touches the heap? The starter replaces the global `operator new`, the function every `new` expression and every growing `std::vector` or `std::string` goes through. The replacement counts each call in `g_heap_allocs` and then gets the memory from `malloc`. `heap_allocs()` returns the count. A check reads it, runs your code, and reads it again: the two numbers must be equal. Leave that part of the starter exactly as it is.

### A ring buffer

A spacecraft is full of places where data arrives faster than it is used for a moment: bytes from a radio, events waiting to be logged, commands waiting to run. Each needs a queue, and a flight queue cannot grow. It has a fixed number of slots.

Picture a rotating sushi counter with 8 plates. The cook puts plates down just behind the last one, and diners take the plate at the front. The counter goes round, so when the cook reaches the end of the track he carries on at its start. Nothing ever moves along; only the two places, front and back, move round.

A **ring buffer** (also called a circular buffer) is that counter in memory: an array of N slots used as a first-in, first-out queue, where the front and back positions wrap from the last slot to slot 0.

### Keeping track: the head and the count

You need two numbers. This project keeps:

- `head_`: the index of the oldest item, the front of the queue;
- `count_`: how many items are held.

The back, where the next item goes, is not stored. It is `(head_ + count_) % N`. The `%` is the remainder after dividing by N, and it does the wrapping: with N = 8, a head of 6 and a count of 3, the next free slot is (6 + 3) % 8 = 1.

Here is a ring of 4 chars, and what happens to it:

| step | action | slots 0 1 2 3 | head | count |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | add A, B, C | A B C . | 0 | 3 |
| 2 | take one (A) | . B C . | 1 | 2 |
| 3 | add D, E | E B C D | 1 | 4 |
| 4 | take one (B) | E . C D | 2 | 3 |

At step 3, E lands in slot (1 + 3) % 4 = 0: the back wrapped round. After step 4, the queue from oldest to newest is C, D, E, found at (2 + 0) % 4, (2 + 1) % 4 and (2 + 2) % 4.

### The alternatives, and why not them

- **A head and a tail index, and nothing else.** Then an empty ring and a full ring both have head equal to tail, and you cannot tell them apart. The classic fix leaves one slot always empty, so a ring of N holds only N − 1 items. With a count, all N slots are used, and "empty" (count 0) and "full" (count N) are different numbers.
- **Shifting the items forward after each take**, like a list. That costs O(n) per take. The ring never moves an item.
- **A linked list with nodes from the heap.** It breaks rule 1, and it scatters the items around memory.

### The invariant, and why every operation keeps it

**Invariant:** 0 ≤ `count_` ≤ N, and the items, oldest first, are at `(head_ + i) % N` for i = 0, 1, …, `count_` − 1.

- **Adding** when `count_` < N writes slot `(head_ + count_) % N`, which is exactly position i = `count_` in the list, then adds one to the count. The old items did not move, so the list is the old list with the new item at the back.
- **Taking** when `count_` > 0 reads slot `head_`, which is position 0: the oldest. Then `head_` becomes `(head_ + 1) % N` and the count drops by one. The item that was at position i is now at position i − 1, so the order is kept.
- Nothing else changes `head_` or `count_`, so the invariant holds after any sequence of operations.

**Cost:** every operation is a few arithmetic steps and one copy of an item: O(1), whatever N is. The memory is N items plus two numbers, fixed when the program is built.

### When the ring is full: two policies

What should adding do when every slot is taken? It depends on what the data is.

- **Refuse.** For commands, silently losing one is the worst outcome. `push` returns `Status::Full` and changes nothing; the caller decides.
- **Overwrite the oldest.** For an event history, the newest events matter most, and logging must never fail. `push_overwrite` writes the new item over the oldest one, moves the head one place on, and counts the loss in `dropped_`, so the loss is never silent.

Both belong in the same class. Picking the policy is the caller's decision, made where the meaning of the data is known.

### How to test a ring buffer

Most ring buffer bugs only appear **after the indices wrap**, so a test that adds three items and takes three proves almost nothing. Good tests:

- fill it, check that one more add is refused, then drain it and check the order;
- run thousands of mixed adds and takes against a **model**, a simple structure that is obviously right (here, a big plain array with two counters), comparing after every step;
- the smallest ring, capacity 1, where head and back are always the same slot;
- null output pointers, and taking from an empty ring.

### Where it is used

- The Linux kernel's `kfifo`, which carries bytes between device drivers and the rest of the kernel.
- Serial ports and radios: the hardware drops bytes into a ring and software takes them out when it has time.
- Audio: a sound card plays from a ring of samples while the program refills the part already played.
- Flight software: the event history, telemetry queues and command queues in frameworks such as NASA's [[core Flight System|cfs]].

**Watch out:** forgetting the `% N` in one place. `items_[head_ + count_]` works perfectly for the first N adds and then writes past the end of the array, into whatever member comes next. The tests that fill and drain once pass; the long mixed test catches it. Also watch the full ring in `push_overwrite`: the new item goes into the **oldest** slot, `head_`, and then the head moves on. Overwriting the newest slot instead keeps a stale item and loses the fresh one.

::: context pot-capstone Rules written for a reason
Gerard Holzmann of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory published "The Power of Ten" in 2006: ten rules for safety-critical code. Each one answers a bug that kept happening in real missions. Rule 1 bans recursion, rule 2 demands a fixed bound on every loop, rule 3 bans dynamic memory after start-up, and rule 7 says to check every return value and every argument. Code for the Curiosity rover was written under rules like these. You met them in Systems Programming; here you build a whole system that obeys them.
:::

::: context fragmentation When free memory is not enough
Imagine a car park where cars of different lengths come and go all day. After a while there is plenty of empty kerb in total, but only in short gaps between parked cars, so a long van finds no space. A heap does the same: blocks freed at different times leave holes, and a big request can fail although the free bytes add up to far more than it needs. On a desktop you restart the program. On a spacecraft six months into its mission, you cannot.
:::

::: context cfs Flight software you can read
NASA's core Flight System (cFS) is open source and flies on many missions, from small satellites to the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. It is written in C, as a set of applications that talk through a software bus, and it follows the same habits as this project: fixed-size tables, status codes on every call, and telemetry in CCSDS packets. JPL's F Prime framework, which flew on the Ingenuity Mars helicopter, does the same in C++. Reading either after this capstone, you will recognise most of what you see.
:::
--- task
The starter has the header comment with the rules, the `Status` list and the heap watch. Keep them. Write:

1. `const char* status_name(Status s)`: the name of each code in capitals, with words separated by `_`: `Status::Ok` gives `"OK"`, `Status::NotImpl` gives `"NOT_IMPL"`, `Status::BadCrc` gives `"BAD_CRC"`, `Status::UnknownApid` gives `"UNKNOWN_APID"`, and so on for all 20 codes. The name of each is its enumerator split into words: `OUT_OF_RANGE`, `NOT_READY`, `TOO_SHORT` and so on. A value that is not in the list gives `"UNKNOWN"`.
2. The class template `RingBuffer<T, N>`, a first-in, first-out queue of at most `N` items of type `T`, kept in a plain array inside the object (no heap). Use `head_` and `count_` as the lesson did. Its members:
   - `Status push(const T& v)`: add `v` at the back. If the ring is full, return `Status::Full` and change nothing.
   - `bool push_overwrite(const T& v)`: add `v` at the back; if the ring is full, drop the oldest item to make room. Return `true` when an item was dropped, `false` otherwise.
   - `Status pop(T* out)`: take the oldest item out into `*out`. `Status::BadArg` if `out` is null, `Status::Empty` if there is nothing to take.
   - `Status peek(T* out) const`: like `pop`, but the item stays.
   - `Status at(std::size_t i, T* out) const`: copy the `i`-th oldest item (0 is the oldest) into `*out`. `Status::BadArg` if `out` is null, `Status::NotFound` if `i` is not less than the size.
   - `void clear()`: empty the ring.
   - `std::size_t size() const`, `bool empty() const`, `bool full() const`, and `static constexpr std::size_t capacity()`, which returns `N`.
   - `std::uint32_t dropped() const`: how many items `push_overwrite` has dropped since the ring was made.

On every failure, nothing in the ring changes.
--- starter
// ============================================================================
// ORBIT flight software core
// Rules, as on a real spacecraft:
//   - no heap allocation after start-up: fixed-size pools and static arrays
//   - no exceptions, no recursion
//   - every function checks its inputs and returns a status code
// ============================================================================
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>

// ---- Status codes: the project's whole error vocabulary ---------------------
// The numbers go into acknowledgement packets, so never reorder them.
enum class Status : std::uint8_t {
    Ok = 0,
    NotImpl,      // a stub: not written yet
    BadArg,       // an input is null or out of range
    Full,         // a fixed-capacity container has no room
    Empty,        // nothing to take out
    NotFound,     // no such key, id or handle
    NoSpace,      // an output buffer is too small, or a pool is used up
    Duplicate,    // the same thing twice
    OutOfRange,   // a result does not fit its type
    NotReady,     // called before set-up finished
    TooShort,     // fewer bytes than the format needs
    BadVersion,   // a packet version we do not speak
    BadType,      // the wrong kind of packet
    BadLength,    // a length field that cannot be right
    BadCrc,       // the checksum does not match
    UnknownApid,  // a packet for an application we do not have
    BadOpcode,    // no such command
    BadArgs,      // a command's arguments are wrong
    Forbidden,    // not allowed in the current mode
    Overrun,      // a frame ran out of time
};

// Returns the code's name in capitals, as the comments above spell it:
// "OK", "NOT_IMPL", "BAD_ARG", ... "OVERRUN". Anything else is "UNKNOWN".
const char* status_name(Status s) {
    return "?";
}

// ---- Heap watch: counts every operator new, so the checks can prove that ----
// ---- the flight code never touches the heap. Leave it as it is. -------------
static long long g_heap_allocs = 0;

void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    ++g_heap_allocs;
    void* p = std::malloc(n == 0 ? 1 : n);
    if (p == nullptr) std::abort();
    return p;
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }

long long heap_allocs() { return g_heap_allocs; }

// ---- RingBuffer: a first-in, first-out queue of fixed capacity --------------
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class RingBuffer {
    static_assert(N > 0, "a ring buffer needs room for at least one item");

public:
    Status push(const T& v) { return Status::NotImpl; }
    bool push_overwrite(const T& v) { return false; }
    Status pop(T* out) { return Status::NotImpl; }
    Status peek(T* out) const { return Status::NotImpl; }
    Status at(std::size_t i, T* out) const { return Status::NotImpl; }
    void clear() {}

    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() { return N; }
    bool empty() const { return false; }
    bool full() const { return false; }
    std::uint32_t dropped() const { return 0; }

private:
    T items_[N] = {};
};
--- solution
// ============================================================================
// ORBIT flight software core
// Rules, as on a real spacecraft:
//   - no heap allocation after start-up: fixed-size pools and static arrays
//   - no exceptions, no recursion
//   - every function checks its inputs and returns a status code
// ============================================================================
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>

// ---- Status codes: the project's whole error vocabulary ---------------------
// The numbers go into acknowledgement packets, so never reorder them.
enum class Status : std::uint8_t {
    Ok = 0,
    NotImpl,      // a stub: not written yet
    BadArg,       // an input is null or out of range
    Full,         // a fixed-capacity container has no room
    Empty,        // nothing to take out
    NotFound,     // no such key, id or handle
    NoSpace,      // an output buffer is too small, or a pool is used up
    Duplicate,    // the same thing twice
    OutOfRange,   // a result does not fit its type
    NotReady,     // called before set-up finished
    TooShort,     // fewer bytes than the format needs
    BadVersion,   // a packet version we do not speak
    BadType,      // the wrong kind of packet
    BadLength,    // a length field that cannot be right
    BadCrc,       // the checksum does not match
    UnknownApid,  // a packet for an application we do not have
    BadOpcode,    // no such command
    BadArgs,      // a command's arguments are wrong
    Forbidden,    // not allowed in the current mode
    Overrun,      // a frame ran out of time
};

const char* status_name(Status s) {
    switch (s) {
        case Status::Ok: return "OK";
        case Status::NotImpl: return "NOT_IMPL";
        case Status::BadArg: return "BAD_ARG";
        case Status::Full: return "FULL";
        case Status::Empty: return "EMPTY";
        case Status::NotFound: return "NOT_FOUND";
        case Status::NoSpace: return "NO_SPACE";
        case Status::Duplicate: return "DUPLICATE";
        case Status::OutOfRange: return "OUT_OF_RANGE";
        case Status::NotReady: return "NOT_READY";
        case Status::TooShort: return "TOO_SHORT";
        case Status::BadVersion: return "BAD_VERSION";
        case Status::BadType: return "BAD_TYPE";
        case Status::BadLength: return "BAD_LENGTH";
        case Status::BadCrc: return "BAD_CRC";
        case Status::UnknownApid: return "UNKNOWN_APID";
        case Status::BadOpcode: return "BAD_OPCODE";
        case Status::BadArgs: return "BAD_ARGS";
        case Status::Forbidden: return "FORBIDDEN";
        case Status::Overrun: return "OVERRUN";
    }
    return "UNKNOWN";
}

// ---- Heap watch: counts every operator new, so the checks can prove that ----
// ---- the flight code never touches the heap. Leave it as it is. -------------
static long long g_heap_allocs = 0;

void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    ++g_heap_allocs;
    void* p = std::malloc(n == 0 ? 1 : n);
    if (p == nullptr) std::abort();
    return p;
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }

long long heap_allocs() { return g_heap_allocs; }

// ---- RingBuffer: a first-in, first-out queue of fixed capacity --------------
// Invariant: 0 <= count_ <= N, and the items, oldest first, sit at
// (head_ + 0) % N, (head_ + 1) % N, ..., (head_ + count_ - 1) % N.
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class RingBuffer {
    static_assert(N > 0, "a ring buffer needs room for at least one item");

public:
    // Adds v at the back. Full when there is no room: nothing changes.
    Status push(const T& v) {
        if (count_ == N) return Status::Full;
        items_[(head_ + count_) % N] = v;
        ++count_;
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // Adds v at the back; when full, the oldest item is dropped to make room.
    // Returns true when an item was dropped.
    bool push_overwrite(const T& v) {
        if (count_ < N) {
            items_[(head_ + count_) % N] = v;
            ++count_;
            return false;
        }
        items_[head_] = v;          // the oldest slot becomes the newest
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;
        ++dropped_;
        return true;
    }

    // Takes the oldest item out into *out. Empty when there is none.
    Status pop(T* out) {
        if (out == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        if (count_ == 0) return Status::Empty;
        *out = items_[head_];
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;
        --count_;
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // Copies the oldest item into *out without taking it out.
    Status peek(T* out) const {
        if (out == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        if (count_ == 0) return Status::Empty;
        *out = items_[head_];
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // Copies the i-th oldest item (0 is the oldest) into *out.
    Status at(std::size_t i, T* out) const {
        if (out == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        if (i >= count_) return Status::NotFound;
        *out = items_[(head_ + i) % N];
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    void clear() {
        head_ = 0;
        count_ = 0;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return count_; }
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() { return N; }
    bool empty() const { return count_ == 0; }
    bool full() const { return count_ == N; }
    std::uint32_t dropped() const { return dropped_; }

private:
    T items_[N] = {};
    std::size_t head_ = 0;       // index of the oldest item
    std::size_t count_ = 0;      // how many items are held
    std::uint32_t dropped_ = 0;  // items lost to push_overwrite
};
--- hint
Keep three members besides the array: `head_` (where the oldest item is), `count_` (how many there are) and `dropped_`. The next free slot is always `(head_ + count_) % N`, and the oldest is at `head_`.
--- hint
`pop` reads `items_[head_]`, then moves `head_` one place on with `% N` and lowers the count. `at(i)` reads `items_[(head_ + i) % N]`. Check the pointer first, then emptiness or the index.
--- hint
In `push_overwrite`, when the ring is not full, do what `push` does. When it is full, the oldest slot is exactly where the new item goes: write `items_[head_]`, move `head_` on by one with `% N`, and add one to `dropped_`. The count stays at N.

[] { for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) { const char* a = status_name(static_cast<Status>(i)); if (std::strcmp(a, "UNKNOWN") == 0 || std::strcmp(a, "?") == 0) return false; for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) if (std::strcmp(a, status_name(static_cast<Status>(j))) == 0) return false; } return std::strcmp(status_name(Status::TooShort), "TOO_SHORT") == 0 && std::strcmp(status_name(Status::Forbidden), "FORBIDDEN") == 0; }()

--- check test | Items come out in the order they went in
[] { RingBuffer<int, 4> r; bool ok = r.push(10) == Status::Ok && r.push(20) == Status::Ok && r.push(30) == Status::Ok; int a = 0, b = 0, c = 0; ok = ok && r.pop(&a) == Status::Ok && r.pop(&b) == Status::Ok && r.pop(&c) == Status::Ok; return ok && a == 10 && b == 20 && c == 30 && r.empty(); }()
--- check test | A full ring refuses and changes nothing
[] { RingBuffer<int, 3> r; r.push(1); r.push(2); r.push(3); bool refused = r.push(4) == Status::Full; int x = 0; r.pop(&x); return refused && r.size() == 2 && x == 1 && !r.full(); }()
--- check test | size, empty, full and capacity
[] { RingBuffer<int, 5> r; bool a = r.empty() && !r.full() && r.size() == 0; for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) r.push(i); bool b = r.full() && !r.empty() && r.size() == 5; return a && b && RingBuffer<int, 5>::capacity() == 5 && r.capacity() == 5; }()
--- check test | pop and peek on an empty ring, and null pointers
[] { RingBuffer<int, 2> r; int x = 77; bool a = r.pop(&x) == Status::Empty && r.peek(&x) == Status::Empty && x == 77; r.push(5); bool b = r.pop(nullptr) == Status::BadArg && r.peek(nullptr) == Status::BadArg && r.size() == 1; return a && b; }()
--- check test | peek shows the oldest and leaves it there
[] { RingBuffer<int, 3> r; r.push(8); r.push(9); int x = 0; bool ok = r.peek(&x) == Status::Ok && x == 8 && r.size() == 2; int y = 0; r.pop(&y); return ok && y == 8; }()
--- check test | Thousands of mixed operations match a simple model
[] { RingBuffer<int, 5> r; static int model[20000]; int mh = 0, mt = 0; unsigned x = 12345u; for (int step = 0; step < 20000; step++) { x = x * 1103515245u + 12345u; bool add = ((x >> 16) & 3u) != 0 || mt == mh; if (add) { Status s = r.push(step); bool fits = mt - mh < 5; if (fits) model[mt++] = step; if ((s == Status::Ok) != fits || (!fits && s != Status::Full)) return false; } else { int v = -1; if (r.pop(&v) != Status::Ok || v != model[mh++]) return false; } if (r.size() != static_cast<std::size_t>(mt - mh)) return false; } return true; }()
--- check test | at(i) walks from the oldest, even after the indexes wrap
[] { RingBuffer<int, 4> r; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) r.push(i); int t = 0; r.pop(&t); r.pop(&t); r.push(5); r.push(6); int v[4] = {}; for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) if (r.at(i, &v[i]) != Status::Ok) return false; int y = 0; return v[0] == 3 && v[1] == 4 && v[2] == 5 && v[3] == 6 && r.at(4, &y) == Status::NotFound && r.at(0, nullptr) == Status::BadArg; }()
--- check test | push_overwrite drops the oldest and counts it
[] { RingBuffer<int, 3> r; bool d1 = r.push_overwrite(1) || r.push_overwrite(2) || r.push_overwrite(3); bool d2 = r.push_overwrite(4); bool d3 = r.push_overwrite(5); int a = 0, b = 0, c = 0; r.at(0, &a); r.at(1, &b); r.at(2, &c); return !d1 && d2 && d3 && a == 3 && b == 4 && c == 5 && r.size() == 3 && r.dropped() == 2; }()
--- check test | push_overwrite into a ring with room drops nothing
[] { RingBuffer<int, 4> r; r.push(1); bool d = r.push_overwrite(2); int a = 0, b = 0; r.pop(&a); r.pop(&b); return !d && a == 1 && b == 2 && r.dropped() == 0; }()
--- check test | A ring of capacity 1
[] { RingBuffer<int, 1> r; bool ok = r.push(7) == Status::Ok && r.full() && r.push(8) == Status::Full; bool d = r.push_overwrite(9); int x = 0; ok = ok && r.pop(&x) == Status::Ok && x == 9 && r.empty(); for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { r.push(i); int y = -1; if (r.pop(&y) != Status::Ok || y != i) return false; } return ok && d && r.dropped() == 1; }()
--- check test | clear empties it, and it works again
[] { RingBuffer<int, 3> r; r.push(1); r.push(2); r.pop(nullptr); r.clear(); bool e = r.empty() && r.size() == 0; r.push(4); r.push(5); r.push(6); int x = 0; r.pop(&x); return e && x == 4 && r.size() == 2; }()
--- check test | Works for structs, not only ints
[] { struct Sample { std::uint32_t t; std::int32_t v; }; RingBuffer<Sample, 2> r; r.push({100, -5}); r.push({200, 7}); Sample s = {}; r.pop(&s); return s.t == 100 && s.v == -5; }()
--- check test | Never touches the heap
[] { static RingBuffer<int, 16> r; long long before = heap_allocs(); for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) { r.push_overwrite(i); if (i % 3 == 0) { int x; r.pop(&x); } } return heap_allocs() == before && r.size() == 15; }()


+++ practice | A byte FIFO for a serial port
--- task
A serial port drops each received byte into a small queue, and the software takes them out later. Write it in C style, with a struct and functions:

```cpp fragment
struct ByteFifo {
    std::uint8_t data[8];
    int head;    // index of the oldest byte
    int count;   // how many bytes are held
};
```

- `void fifo_init(ByteFifo* f)`: make it empty.
- `bool fifo_put(ByteFifo* f, std::uint8_t b)`: add `b` at the back and return `true`; return `false` and change nothing if all 8 places are taken.
- `bool fifo_get(ByteFifo* f, std::uint8_t* out)`: take the oldest byte into `*out` and return `true`; return `false` if the FIFO is empty or `out` is null.
- `int fifo_count(const ByteFifo* f)`: how many bytes are held.
--- starter
#include <cstdint>

struct ByteFifo {
    std::uint8_t data[8];
    int head;
    int count;
};

void fifo_init(ByteFifo* f) {
}

bool fifo_put(ByteFifo* f, std::uint8_t b) {
    return false;
}

bool fifo_get(ByteFifo* f, std::uint8_t* out) {
    return false;
}

int fifo_count(const ByteFifo* f) {
    return 0;
}
--- solution
#include <cstdint>

struct ByteFifo {
    std::uint8_t data[8];
    int head;
    int count;
};

void fifo_init(ByteFifo* f) {
    f->head = 0;
    f->count = 0;
}

bool fifo_put(ByteFifo* f, std::uint8_t b) {
    if (f->count == 8) return false;
    f->data[(f->head + f->count) % 8] = b;
    f->count++;
    return true;
}

bool fifo_get(ByteFifo* f, std::uint8_t* out) {
    if (out == nullptr || f->count == 0) return false;
    *out = f->data[f->head];
    f->head = (f->head + 1) % 8;
    f->count--;
    return true;
}

int fifo_count(const ByteFifo* f) {
    return f->count;
}
--- hint
The back of the queue is `(head + count) % 8`; the front is `head`.
--- hint
After taking a byte, move `head` on with `(head + 1) % 8` and lower `count`.
--- check test | Bytes come out in order
[] { ByteFifo f; fifo_init(&f); fifo_put(&f, 0x41); fifo_put(&f, 0x42); std::uint8_t a = 0, b = 0; bool ok = fifo_get(&f, &a) && fifo_get(&f, &b); return ok && a == 0x41 && b == 0x42 && fifo_count(&f) == 0; }()
--- check test | The ninth byte is refused
[] { ByteFifo f; fifo_init(&f); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) if (!fifo_put(&f, i)) return false; std::uint8_t x = 0; bool refused = !fifo_put(&f, 99); fifo_get(&f, &x); return refused && x == 0 && fifo_count(&f) == 7; }()
--- check test | Empty, and a null pointer
[] { ByteFifo f; fifo_init(&f); std::uint8_t x = 5; bool a = !fifo_get(&f, &x) && x == 5; fifo_put(&f, 1); return a && !fifo_get(&f, nullptr) && fifo_count(&f) == 1; }()
--- check test | 1000 bytes through, with the indexes wrapping
[] { ByteFifo f; fifo_init(&f); int next_in = 0, next_out = 0; for (int round = 0; round < 200; round++) { for (int k = 0; k < 5; k++) fifo_put(&f, static_cast<std::uint8_t>(next_in++)); for (int k = 0; k < 5; k++) { std::uint8_t x; if (!fifo_get(&f, &x) || x != static_cast<std::uint8_t>(next_out++)) return false; } } return fifo_count(&f) == 0; }()

+++ practice | Head and tail, with one slot kept empty
--- task
Another common ring keeps two indexes and no count: `head` (where the oldest item is) and `tail` (where the next item goes). With only those two, "empty" and "full" would both mean `head == tail`, so this design never fills the last slot: an array of 5 slots holds at most 4 items.

```cpp fragment
struct Ring5 {
    int slot[5];
    int head;
    int tail;
};
```

Write:

- `void ring_init(Ring5* r)`: empty.
- `bool ring_empty(const Ring5* r)`: `head == tail`.
- `bool ring_full(const Ring5* r)`: the slot after `tail` (wrapping) is `head`.
- `int ring_size(const Ring5* r)`: how many items are held, from `head` and `tail` alone.
- `bool ring_push(Ring5* r, int v)` and `bool ring_pop(Ring5* r, int* out)`: `false` when full, or when empty (or `out` is null).
--- starter
struct Ring5 {
    int slot[5];
    int head;
    int tail;
};

void ring_init(Ring5* r) {
}

bool ring_empty(const Ring5* r) {
    return true;
}

bool ring_full(const Ring5* r) {
    return false;
}

int ring_size(const Ring5* r) {
    return 0;
}

bool ring_push(Ring5* r, int v) {
    return false;
}

bool ring_pop(Ring5* r, int* out) {
    return false;
}
--- solution
struct Ring5 {
    int slot[5];
    int head;
    int tail;
};

void ring_init(Ring5* r) {
    r->head = 0;
    r->tail = 0;
}

bool ring_empty(const Ring5* r) {
    return r->head == r->tail;
}

bool ring_full(const Ring5* r) {
    return (r->tail + 1) % 5 == r->head;
}

// tail - head can be negative after tail wraps; adding 5 first keeps it in 0..4.
int ring_size(const Ring5* r) {
    return (r->tail - r->head + 5) % 5;
}

bool ring_push(Ring5* r, int v) {
    if (ring_full(r)) return false;
    r->slot[r->tail] = v;
    r->tail = (r->tail + 1) % 5;
    return true;
}

bool ring_pop(Ring5* r, int* out) {
    if (out == nullptr || ring_empty(r)) return false;
    *out = r->slot[r->head];
    r->head = (r->head + 1) % 5;
    return true;
}
--- hint
Full means one more push would make `tail` equal `head`: test `(tail + 1) % 5 == head`.
--- hint
For the size, `tail - head` is right until `tail` wraps round below `head`. Add 5 before taking `% 5`, so the value is never negative.
--- check test | Holds exactly 4 items
[] { Ring5 r; ring_init(&r); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) if (!ring_push(&r, i)) return false; return ring_full(&r) && !ring_push(&r, 9) && ring_size(&r) == 4; }()
--- check test | First in, first out
[] { Ring5 r; ring_init(&r); ring_push(&r, 7); ring_push(&r, 8); int a = 0, b = 0; ring_pop(&r, &a); ring_pop(&r, &b); return a == 7 && b == 8 && ring_empty(&r) && ring_size(&r) == 0; }()
--- check test | The size is right after tail wraps below head
[] { Ring5 r; ring_init(&r); int x; for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) ring_push(&r, i); ring_pop(&r, &x); ring_pop(&r, &x); ring_pop(&r, &x); ring_push(&r, 10); ring_push(&r, 11); return r.tail < r.head && ring_size(&r) == 3 && !ring_full(&r); }()
--- check test | Empty and null
[] { Ring5 r; ring_init(&r); int x = 3; bool a = !ring_pop(&r, &x) && x == 3; ring_push(&r, 1); return a && !ring_pop(&r, nullptr) && ring_size(&r) == 1; }()
--- check test | Long run in order
[] { Ring5 r; ring_init(&r); int in = 0, out = 0; for (int k = 0; k < 500; k++) { while (ring_push(&r, in)) in++; int x; for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++) { if (!ring_pop(&r, &x) || x != out++) return false; } } return ring_size(&r) == in - out; }()

+++ practice | The last five commands, newest first
--- task
The ground console keeps the last five commands the operator typed, and shows them newest first. Each command is a small number (its opcode). Use a ring that overwrites the oldest when full:

```cpp fragment
struct History {
    int op[5];
    int head;    // the oldest
    int count;
};
```

- `void hist_init(History* h)`.
- `void hist_add(History* h, int opcode)`: add it; when there are already five, the oldest is forgotten.
- `int hist_show(const History* h, char* buf, int size)`: write the opcodes held, **newest first**, into `buf` with `snprintf`, as numbers separated by single spaces (`"9 8 7"`), and return what `snprintf` returned for the whole text. With nothing held, write the empty text and return 0.

Build the text piece by piece: keep how many characters are written so far, and stop adding if the buffer is already full.
--- starter
#include <cstdio>

struct History {
    int op[5];
    int head;
    int count;
};

void hist_init(History* h) {
}

void hist_add(History* h, int opcode) {
}

int hist_show(const History* h, char* buf, int size) {
    return 0;
}
--- solution
#include <cstdio>

struct History {
    int op[5];
    int head;
    int count;
};

void hist_init(History* h) {
    h->head = 0;
    h->count = 0;
}

void hist_add(History* h, int opcode) {
    if (h->count < 5) {
        h->op[(h->head + h->count) % 5] = opcode;
        h->count++;
    } else {
        h->op[h->head] = opcode;   // the oldest slot takes the newest command
        h->head = (h->head + 1) % 5;
    }
}

int hist_show(const History* h, char* buf, int size) {
    if (size > 0) buf[0] = '\0';
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = h->count - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        int v = h->op[(h->head + i) % 5];
        const char* sep = i == h->count - 1 ? "" : " ";
        int room = total < size ? size - total : 0;
        int n = snprintf(room > 0 ? buf + total : nullptr, room, "%s%d", sep, v);
        total += n;
    }
    return total;
}
--- hint
The newest item is at position `count - 1`, which is slot `(head + count - 1) % 5`. Walk the positions from `count - 1` down to 0.
--- hint
Keep `total`, the length written so far. Each piece goes to `buf + total` with room `size - total`; when there is no room left, pass a null pointer and room 0, and `snprintf` still tells you the length it needed.
--- check test | Newest first
[] { History h; hist_init(&h); hist_add(&h, 3); hist_add(&h, 14); hist_add(&h, 15); char b[64]; int n = hist_show(&h, b, sizeof b); return std::string(b) == "15 14 3" && n == 7; }()
--- check test | Only the last five are kept
[] { History h; hist_init(&h); for (int i = 1; i <= 8; i++) hist_add(&h, i); char b[64]; hist_show(&h, b, sizeof b); return std::string(b) == "8 7 6 5 4"; }()
--- check test | Nothing held
[] { History h; hist_init(&h); char b[8] = "xx"; int n = hist_show(&h, b, sizeof b); return n == 0 && b[0] == '\0'; }()
--- check test | A small buffer is cut short but the full length comes back
[] { History h; hist_init(&h); hist_add(&h, 100); hist_add(&h, 200); hist_add(&h, 300); char b[6]; int n = hist_show(&h, b, sizeof b); return std::string(b) == "300 2" && n == 11; }()

+++ practice | Taking many items at once
--- task
A radio driver empties a ring buffer in one go, into a caller's array. Here is the ring:

```cpp fragment
struct Ring {
    int items[6];
    int head;
    int count;
};
```

Write `int take_many(Ring* r, int* out, int max)`: move up to `max` items, oldest first, into `out[0]`, `out[1]`, ..., remove them from the ring, and return how many were moved. It must be right when the items wrap round the end of the array. Return 0 and change nothing if `out` is null or `max` is 0 or less. Taking from an empty ring returns 0.
--- starter
struct Ring {
    int items[6];
    int head;
    int count;
};

int take_many(Ring* r, int* out, int max) {
    int n = 0;
    while (n < max) {
        out[n] = r->items[r->head + n];
        n++;
    }
    return n;
}
--- solution
struct Ring {
    int items[6];
    int head;
    int count;
};

int take_many(Ring* r, int* out, int max) {
    if (out == nullptr || max <= 0) return 0;
    int n = max < r->count ? max : r->count;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) out[i] = r->items[(r->head + i) % 6];
    r->head = (r->head + n) % 6;
    r->count -= n;
    return n;
}
--- hint
You can take at most `count` items: work out `n`, the smaller of `max` and `count`, before the loop.
--- hint
Item `i` of the queue is at `(head + i) % 6`. After the loop, move `head` on by `n` with `% 6` and lower `count` by `n`.
--- check test | Takes what fits, in order
[] { Ring r = {{10, 11, 12, 0, 0, 0}, 0, 3}; int out[6] = {}; int n = take_many(&r, out, 2); return n == 2 && out[0] == 10 && out[1] == 11 && r.count == 1 && r.head == 2; }()
--- check test | Across the end of the array
[] { Ring r = {{40, 50, 0, 0, 20, 30}, 4, 4}; int out[6] = {}; int n = take_many(&r, out, 6); return n == 4 && out[0] == 20 && out[1] == 30 && out[2] == 40 && out[3] == 50 && r.count == 0 && r.head == 2; }()
--- check test | Empty ring
[] { Ring r = {{0}, 3, 0}; int out[2] = {7, 7}; return take_many(&r, out, 2) == 0 && out[0] == 7 && r.head == 3; }()
--- check test | max of 0 or less, and a null output
[] { Ring r = {{1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0}, 0, 3}; int out[3]; return take_many(&r, out, 0) == 0 && take_many(&r, out, -2) == 0 && take_many(&r, nullptr, 3) == 0 && r.count == 3; }()

+++ practice | Debug: the event log that forgets the wrong event
--- task
This ring keeps the newest 4 temperature readings. When it is full, adding a reading should drop the **oldest** one. But after a few extra readings, the log shows a stale reading and the newest ones are missing. Find the bug in `log_add` and fix it. Everything else is right.
--- starter
struct TempLog {
    int reading[4];
    int head;
    int count;
};

void log_init(TempLog* t) {
    t->head = 0;
    t->count = 0;
}

void log_add(TempLog* t, int v) {
    if (t->count < 4) {
        t->reading[(t->head + t->count) % 4] = v;
        t->count++;
        return;
    }
    t->reading[(t->head + t->count - 1) % 4] = v;
}

// The i-th oldest reading.
int log_get(const TempLog* t, int i) {
    return t->reading[(t->head + i) % 4];
}
--- solution
struct TempLog {
    int reading[4];
    int head;
    int count;
};

void log_init(TempLog* t) {
    t->head = 0;
    t->count = 0;
}

void log_add(TempLog* t, int v) {
    if (t->count < 4) {
        t->reading[(t->head + t->count) % 4] = v;
        t->count++;
        return;
    }
    // Full: the oldest slot takes the new reading, and the next one becomes the oldest.
    t->reading[t->head] = v;
    t->head = (t->head + 1) % 4;
}

// The i-th oldest reading.
int log_get(const TempLog* t, int i) {
    return t->reading[(t->head + i) % 4];
}
--- hint
When full, which slot holds the oldest reading? It is not the one the code writes to.
--- hint
Write into `reading[head]`, then move `head` one place on, so the reading after it becomes the oldest.
--- check test | Two extra readings drop the two oldest
[] { TempLog t; log_init(&t); for (int v = 1; v <= 6; v++) log_add(&t, v); return log_get(&t, 0) == 3 && log_get(&t, 1) == 4 && log_get(&t, 2) == 5 && log_get(&t, 3) == 6; }()
--- check test | Many extra readings keep the newest four in order
[] { TempLog t; log_init(&t); for (int v = 0; v < 103; v++) log_add(&t, v); return log_get(&t, 0) == 99 && log_get(&t, 3) == 102 && t.count == 4; }()
--- check test | Before it fills, nothing is dropped
[] { TempLog t; log_init(&t); log_add(&t, 20); log_add(&t, 21); log_add(&t, 22); return t.count == 3 && log_get(&t, 0) == 20 && log_get(&t, 2) == 22; }()

+++ practice | Indexes that never wrap
--- task
Linux's `kfifo` uses a neat trick. The capacity is a power of two, here 8, and the two positions are counters that only ever go up: `in` counts every item ever added and `out` every item ever taken. The slot for a counter is `counter & 7` (the low 3 bits, the same as `% 8` for unsigned numbers). The size is simply `in - out`, and this stays right even when the counters pass their largest value and wrap to 0, because unsigned subtraction works modulo 2 to the 16.

```cpp fragment
struct Fifo {
    int slot[8];
    std::uint16_t in;    // items ever added, mod 65536
    std::uint16_t out;   // items ever taken, mod 65536
};
```

Write:

- `std::uint16_t fifo_size(const Fifo* f)`: `in - out`, as a `std::uint16_t` (cast the result: arithmetic on `uint16_t` happens in `int`).
- `bool fifo_push(Fifo* f, int v)`: `false` if 8 items are held; otherwise store at `slot[in & 7]` and add one to `in`.
- `bool fifo_pop(Fifo* f, int* out)`: `false` if empty or `out` is null; otherwise read `slot[out & 7]` and add one to `out`.

The checks push and pop 200,000 items, so both counters wrap round several times.
--- starter
#include <cstdint>

struct Fifo {
    int slot[8];
    std::uint16_t in;
    std::uint16_t out;
};

std::uint16_t fifo_size(const Fifo* f) {
    return 0;
}

bool fifo_push(Fifo* f, int v) {
    return false;
}

bool fifo_pop(Fifo* f, int* out) {
    return false;
}
--- solution
#include <cstdint>

struct Fifo {
    int slot[8];
    std::uint16_t in;
    std::uint16_t out;
};

// Unsigned subtraction is modulo 65536, so this is right across a wrap.
std::uint16_t fifo_size(const Fifo* f) {
    return static_cast<std::uint16_t>(f->in - f->out);
}

bool fifo_push(Fifo* f, int v) {
    if (fifo_size(f) == 8) return false;
    f->slot[f->in & 7u] = v;
    f->in = static_cast<std::uint16_t>(f->in + 1);
    return true;
}

bool fifo_pop(Fifo* f, int* out) {
    if (out == nullptr || fifo_size(f) == 0) return false;
    *out = f->slot[f->out & 7u];
    f->out = static_cast<std::uint16_t>(f->out + 1);
    return true;
}
--- hint
`f->in - f->out` is computed as an `int`, which can be negative right after `in` wraps to 0. Casting it back to `std::uint16_t` keeps the low 16 bits, which is the right count.
--- hint
Adding one to a `std::uint16_t` also happens in `int`: cast back, `static_cast<std::uint16_t>(f->in + 1)`, so 65535 + 1 becomes 0.
--- check test | Fills to 8, then refuses
[] { Fifo f = {}; for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) if (!fifo_push(&f, i)) return false; return !fifo_push(&f, 99) && fifo_size(&f) == 8; }()
--- check test | Right across the counters' wrap
[] { Fifo f = {}; f.in = 65534; f.out = 65534; for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) fifo_push(&f, i * 10); int a = 0, b = 0; fifo_pop(&f, &a); fifo_pop(&f, &b); return f.in == 3 && fifo_size(&f) == 3 && a == 0 && b == 10; }()
--- check test | 200,000 items in order
[] { Fifo f = {}; int next_in = 0, next_out = 0; for (int round = 0; round < 40000; round++) { for (int k = 0; k < 5; k++) if (!fifo_push(&f, next_in++)) return false; for (int k = 0; k < 5; k++) { int x; if (!fifo_pop(&f, &x) || x != next_out++) return false; } } return fifo_size(&f) == 0 && f.in == static_cast<std::uint16_t>(200000); }()
--- check test | Empty and null
[] { Fifo f = {}; int x = 1; bool a = !fifo_pop(&f, &x) && x == 1; fifo_push(&f, 4); return a && !fifo_pop(&f, nullptr) && fifo_size(&f) == 1; }()

=== cap-flight-02 | Milestone 2: a pool of fixed blocks, and packet queues that share it
--- teach
Last milestone's ring buffer copies each item into its own array. That is right for small items. A telemetry packet is up to 128 bytes, and on its way down it may sit in a queue, move to another, and be copied into the radio's buffer: every hop would copy all 128 bytes. Worse, a spacecraft has several queues (urgent packets, routine packets), and memory set aside for one queue sits idle while another overflows. This milestone builds the flight answer to `new` and `delete`: a **pool** of fixed-size blocks, handed out by **handles**, and a packet queue that holds only handles.

### A pool

Picture a cloakroom with 24 numbered hooks. You hand over a coat and get a ticket; later the ticket gets the coat back. The attendant never runs out of floor space in the middle of the evening, because the hooks were counted before the doors opened. She also keeps the free hooks in a pile of tickets, so finding a free hook takes no searching.

A **pool** (or pool allocator) is a fixed array of N blocks of the same size, all created at start-up, plus a record of which are free. **Acquiring** takes a free block; **releasing** gives it back. It is the allocator of choice in flight software because both operations take a fixed, small time, and it cannot fragment: every block is the same size, so any free block fits any request.

### The free list, threaded through the indexes

You built free lists in Systems Programming, with pointers stored inside the free blocks. This pool stores them in a separate array of indexes, `next_`, so the blocks' own bytes are never overwritten:

- `free_head_` is the index of the first free block; the value N means "none".
- `next_[i]` is the free block after block i.

At start-up the list is 0 → 1 → 2 → … → N − 1 → N (the end). Acquiring takes the head: `i = free_head_; free_head_ = next_[i];`. Releasing block i puts it back in front: `next_[i] = free_head_; free_head_ = i;`. So the free list is a stack, and the block released last is handed out first. That is on purpose: its bytes are probably still in the CPU's [[cache|cache-warm]], and the order is completely predictable, which the tests rely on.

**Cost:** acquire and release each change two numbers: O(1). Memory: the N blocks plus a few bytes of bookkeeping per block.

### Why handles, not pointers

`malloc` returns a pointer, and a pointer cannot tell you that its block was already freed. In C, using a freed block, or freeing it twice, silently corrupts memory. A pool can do better. It hands out a **handle**: the block's index plus a **generation**, a counter stored with each block that goes up by one every time the block is released.

```cpp fragment
struct Handle {
    std::uint16_t index;   // which block
    std::uint16_t gen;     // which "lifetime" of that block
};
```

A handle is **valid** when its index is in range, the block is in use, and the block's generation equals the handle's. After a release, the block's generation moves on, so every copy of the old handle stops working: `get` returns null and `release` refuses it. A double release is caught the same way. Generation 0 is never used, so a handle of all zeros (or `kNoHandle`) is never valid.

A 16-bit generation wraps after 65,535 releases of the same block. From 65,535 it goes to 1, skipping 0. A stale handle could then look valid again, but only if it was kept while its block was reused 65,535 times: a risk small enough to accept, and an example of the [[ABA problem|aba]].

Alternatives, and why not:

- **Raw pointers into the pool:** fast, but no detection of stale use.
- **Reference counting:** every copy costs an increment, and a forgotten decrement leaks a block forever.
- **A bitmap of free blocks:** tiny, but acquiring means scanning for a zero bit, O(N) in the worst case.

### The invariant

Every block index is in exactly one of two places: **in use**, or **on the free list, once**. `in_use_` counts the first group.

- Acquire takes the head off the free list and marks it in use: one block moves from the list to "in use".
- Release first checks the handle is valid, so the block is in use and therefore not on the list; then it pushes it on. It can never appear twice.

Since no index is ever on the list twice, no block is ever handed out twice. That is the pool's whole promise, and the validity check on release is what keeps it.

Two more numbers help the people who size the pool: the **high-water mark** (the most blocks ever in use at once) and the count of **failures** (acquires refused because nothing was free). You run the system in test, read the high-water mark, and size the pool with a margin.

### Packet queues that share one pool

A `PacketQueue<Depth>` is a ring buffer of handles, plus a pointer to a shared `BufferPool` (24 blocks of 128 bytes). Two queues can share one pool:

- `put` checks that the queue has room, acquires a block, copies the packet in, and pushes the handle;
- `take` peeks at the oldest handle, copies the packet out, then pops it and releases the block.

The order of those steps matters. If `put` acquired a block and only then found the queue full, the block would never be released: a **leak**, and the pool would shrink by one block for every refusal. If `take` released the block before copying, a later acquire could reuse it while you still read it. Check first, act last.

What if the caller's buffer is too small for the packet? `take` returns `NoSpace` and leaves the packet queued, so nothing is lost; the caller can come back with a bigger buffer.

### How big should the pool be?

If the pool has at least as many blocks as all its queues' depths added up, `NoSpace` can never happen: every queue can fill at once. Sizing for the average and hoping queues do not peak together saves memory, and is exactly the kind of bet that fails on the day everything goes wrong at once. Flight software sizes for the worst case, and measures the high-water mark to confirm it.

### How to test it

- acquire all N blocks, check the order of indexes, check one more is refused and counted as a failure;
- release one and acquire again: the same index comes back with the next generation;
- release twice, release a stale handle, release a handle with a made-up index: all refused, nothing changes;
- cycle one block 65,536 times to cross the generation wrap;
- for queues, check that `pool.in_use()` always equals the number of queued packets. If it is bigger, something leaked.

### Where it is used

- Real-time operating systems such as FreeRTOS, VxWorks and RTEMS all offer fixed-block memory pools for exactly this reason.
- The Linux kernel's [[slab allocator|slab]] keeps pools of same-sized objects.
- Game engines use handles with generations for their entities, so a reference to a destroyed monster fails safely.
- Network stacks keep packets in pooled buffers and pass handles between layers.

**Watch out:** acquiring a block before checking that the queue has room. Every refused `put` then leaks one block, and after 24 refusals the pool is empty and every queue that shares it stops working. The symptom appears far from the cause, hours later. The check `pool.in_use() == queued packets` finds it at once.

::: context cache-warm Why the last block freed is the best one to reuse
A CPU keeps recently used memory in small, fast caches near the core. Reading a byte already in the cache takes a few cycles; reading one from main memory takes a hundred or more. The block that was released a moment ago was probably just used, so it is likely still cached. Handing it out again first is free speed. A queue-ordered free list would reuse the block used longest ago, which is the least likely to be cached.
:::

::: context aba When A comes back
The ABA problem is named after a value that changes from A to B and back to A: a check that only compares "is it still A?" wrongly concludes nothing happened. Here the value is the generation. It is best known in lock-free programming, where a thread reads a pointer, another thread frees and reuses that memory, and the first thread's compare-and-swap succeeds on memory that is now something else. Wider counters make it rarer; they cannot make it impossible.
:::

::: context slab Pools inside Linux
Jeff Bonwick designed the slab allocator for Solaris in 1994, and Linux adopted the idea. The kernel creates a cache for each common object type, such as the structures for open files or network packets, and carves pages of memory into slots of exactly that size. Allocating one is taking a free slot from a list; freeing puts it back. Because each cache holds one kind of object, freed objects can even keep their initialised state, which saves setting them up again next time.
:::
--- task
The starter declares `Handle`, `kNoHandle`, the packet buffer constants and `BufferPool`. Write the rest.

**`Pool<T, N>`**, with the free list and generations as the lesson described:

- The constructor calls `reset()`. `reset()` makes every block free, with the free list in index order (0 first), and adds one to every block's generation (from 65535 it goes to 1; a new pool's blocks start at generation 1). So every old handle stops working. `reset` does not change the high-water mark or the failure count, which are totals since the pool was made.
- `Status acquire(Handle* out)`: `BadArg` if `out` is null. If no block is free, add one to the failure count and return `NoSpace`. Otherwise take the block at the head of the free list, set its item to `T{}`, mark it in use, update the high-water mark, and write `{index, generation}` into `*out`.
- `Status release(Handle h)`: `BadArg` (and nothing changes) unless `valid(h)`. Otherwise mark the block free, add one to its generation (65535 goes to 1), and push it on the front of the free list.
- `bool valid(Handle h) const`: the index is below N, the generation is not 0, the block is in use, and its generation equals `h.gen`.
- `T* get(Handle h)` and its `const` version: the block's item, or `nullptr` if the handle is not valid.
- `in_use()`, `available()` (N minus in use), `high_water()`, `failures()` and `capacity()` (N).

**`PacketQueue<Depth>`**, a FIFO of up to `Depth` packets whose bytes live in blocks of the shared pool:

- `Status put(const std::uint8_t* bytes, std::size_t len)`: `BadArg` if the pool pointer or `bytes` is null, or `len` is 0 or more than `kMaxPacketBytes`. `Full` if the queue already holds `Depth` packets. If the pool has no free block, return what `acquire` returned (`NoSpace`). Otherwise copy the bytes and the length into the block and queue its handle. On any failure nothing is queued and no block is left in use.
- `Status take(std::uint8_t* out, std::size_t cap, std::size_t* len)`: `BadArg` if any pointer is null; `Empty` if nothing is queued; `NoSpace` if the oldest packet is longer than `cap`, and then it stays queued. Otherwise copy it into `out`, write its length into `*len`, remove it and release its block.
- `Status front_len(std::size_t* len) const`: the length of the oldest packet, without taking it (`BadArg`, `Empty` as above).
- `std::size_t size() const` and `bool empty() const`.

// ============================================================================
// ORBIT flight software core
// Rules, as on a real spacecraft:
//   - no heap allocation after start-up: fixed-size pools and static arrays
//   - no exceptions, no recursion
//   - every function checks its inputs and returns a status code
// ============================================================================
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>

// ---- Status codes: the project's whole error vocabulary ---------------------
// The numbers go into acknowledgement packets, so never reorder them.
enum class Status : std::uint8_t {
    Ok = 0,
    NotImpl,      // a stub: not written yet
    BadArg,       // an input is null or out of range
    Full,         // a fixed-capacity container has no room
    Empty,        // nothing to take out
    NotFound,     // no such key, id or handle
    NoSpace,      // an output buffer is too small, or a pool is used up
    Duplicate,    // the same thing twice
    OutOfRange,   // a result does not fit its type
    NotReady,     // called before set-up finished
    TooShort,     // fewer bytes than the format needs
    BadVersion,   // a packet version we do not speak
    BadType,      // the wrong kind of packet
    BadLength,    // a length field that cannot be right
    BadCrc,       // the checksum does not match
    UnknownApid,  // a packet for an application we do not have
    BadOpcode,    // no such command
    BadArgs,      // a command's arguments are wrong
    Forbidden,    // not allowed in the current mode
    Overrun,      // a frame ran out of time
};

const char* status_name(Status s) {
    switch (s) {
        case Status::Ok: return "OK";
        case Status::NotImpl: return "NOT_IMPL";
        case Status::BadArg: return "BAD_ARG";
        case Status::Full: return "FULL";
        case Status::Empty: return "EMPTY";
        case Status::NotFound: return "NOT_FOUND";
        case Status::NoSpace: return "NO_SPACE";
        case Status::Duplicate: return "DUPLICATE";
        case Status::OutOfRange: return "OUT_OF_RANGE";
        case Status::NotReady: return "NOT_READY";
        case Status::TooShort: return "TOO_SHORT";
        case Status::BadVersion: return "BAD_VERSION";
        case Status::BadType: return "BAD_TYPE";
        case Status::BadLength: return "BAD_LENGTH";
        case Status::BadCrc: return "BAD_CRC";
        case Status::UnknownApid: return "UNKNOWN_APID";
        case Status::BadOpcode: return "BAD_OPCODE";
        case Status::BadArgs: return "BAD_ARGS";
        case Status::Forbidden: return "FORBIDDEN";
        case Status::Overrun: return "OVERRUN";
    }
    return "UNKNOWN";
}

// ---- Heap watch: counts every operator new, so the checks can prove that ----
// ---- the flight code never touches the heap. Leave it as it is. -------------
static long long g_heap_allocs = 0;

void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    ++g_heap_allocs;
    void* p = std::malloc(n == 0 ? 1 : n);
    if (p == nullptr) std::abort();
    return p;
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }

long long heap_allocs() { return g_heap_allocs; }

// ---- RingBuffer: a first-in, first-out queue of fixed capacity --------------
// Invariant: 0 <= count_ <= N, and the items, oldest first, sit at
// (head_ + 0) % N, (head_ + 1) % N, ..., (head_ + count_ - 1) % N.
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class RingBuffer {
    static_assert(N > 0, "a ring buffer needs room for at least one item");

public:
    // Adds v at the back. Full when there is no room: nothing changes.
    Status push(const T& v) {
        if (count_ == N) return Status::Full;
        items_[(head_ + count_) % N] = v;
        ++count_;
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // Adds v at the back; when full, the oldest item is dropped to make room.
    // Returns true when an item was dropped.
    bool push_overwrite(const T& v) {
        if (count_ < N) {
            items_[(head_ + count_) % N] = v;
            ++count_;
            return false;
        }
        items_[head_] = v;          // the oldest slot becomes the newest
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;
        ++dropped_;
        return true;
    }

    // Takes the oldest item out into *out. Empty when there is none.
    Status pop(T* out) {
        if (out == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        if (count_ == 0) return Status::Empty;
        *out = items_[head_];
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;
        --count_;
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // Copies the oldest item into *out without taking it out.
    Status peek(T* out) const {
        if (out == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        if (count_ == 0) return Status::Empty;
        *out = items_[head_];
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // Copies the i-th oldest item (0 is the oldest) into *out.
    Status at(std::size_t i, T* out) const {
        if (out == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        if (i >= count_) return Status::NotFound;
        *out = items_[(head_ + i) % N];
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    void clear() {
        head_ = 0;
        count_ = 0;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return count_; }
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() { return N; }
    bool empty() const { return count_ == 0; }
    bool full() const { return count_ == N; }
    std::uint32_t dropped() const { return dropped_; }

private:
    T items_[N] = {};
    std::size_t head_ = 0;       // index of the oldest item
    std::size_t count_ = 0;      // how many items are held
    std::uint32_t dropped_ = 0;  // items lost to push_overwrite
};

// ---- Pool: N fixed blocks, handed out and taken back in O(1) ----------------
// A handle names a block by its index and the block's generation. Releasing a
// block bumps its generation, so an old handle to it stops working.
struct Handle {
    std::uint16_t index;
    std::uint16_t gen;   // 0 never names a live block
};

constexpr Handle kNoHandle = {0xFFFF, 0};

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class Pool {
    static_assert(N > 0 && N < 0xFFFF, "a pool holds 1 to 65534 blocks");

public:
    Pool() { reset(); }

    void reset() {}
    Status acquire(Handle* out) { return Status::NotImpl; }
    Status release(Handle h) { return Status::NotImpl; }
    bool valid(Handle h) const { return false; }
    T* get(Handle h) { return nullptr; }
    const T* get(Handle h) const { return nullptr; }

    std::size_t in_use() const { return 0; }
    std::size_t available() const { return 0; }
    std::size_t high_water() const { return 0; }
    std::uint32_t failures() const { return 0; }
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() { return N; }

private:
    T items_[N] = {};
};

// ---- Packet buffers and queues that share one pool --------------------------
constexpr std::size_t kMaxPacketBytes = 128;
constexpr std::size_t kBufferCount = 24;

struct PacketBuffer {
    std::uint8_t bytes[kMaxPacketBytes];
    std::uint16_t len;
};

using BufferPool = Pool<PacketBuffer, kBufferCount>;

template <std::size_t Depth>
class PacketQueue {
public:
    explicit PacketQueue(BufferPool* pool) : pool_(pool) {}

    Status put(const std::uint8_t* bytes, std::size_t len) { return Status::NotImpl; }
    Status take(std::uint8_t* out, std::size_t cap, std::size_t* len) { return Status::NotImpl; }
    Status front_len(std::size_t* len) const { return Status::NotImpl; }
    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    bool empty() const { return false; }
    static constexpr std::size_t depth() { return Depth; }

private:
    BufferPool* pool_;
    RingBuffer<Handle, Depth> fifo_;
};

// ---- RingBuffer: a first-in, first-out queue of fixed capacity --------------
// Invariant: 0 <= count_ <= N, and the items, oldest first, sit at
// (head_ + 0) % N, (head_ + 1) % N, ..., (head_ + count_ - 1) % N.
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class RingBuffer {
    static_assert(N > 0, "a ring buffer needs room for at least one item");

public:
    // Adds v at the back. Full when there is no room: nothing changes.
    Status push(const T& v) {
        if (count_ == N) return Status::Full;
        items_[(head_ + count_) % N] = v;
        ++count_;
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // Adds v at the back; when full, the oldest item is dropped to make room.
    // Returns true when an item was dropped.
    bool push_overwrite(const T& v) {
        if (count_ < N) {
            items_[(head_ + count_) % N] = v;
            ++count_;
            return false;
        }
        items_[head_] = v;          // the oldest slot becomes the newest
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;
        ++dropped_;
        return true;
    }

    // Takes the oldest item out into *out. Empty when there is none.
    Status pop(T* out) {
        if (out == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        if (count_ == 0) return Status::Empty;
        *out = items_[head_];
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;
        --count_;
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // Copies the oldest item into *out without taking it out.
    Status peek(T* out) const {
        if (out == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        if (count_ == 0) return Status::Empty;
        *out = items_[head_];
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // Copies the i-th oldest item (0 is the oldest) into *out.
    Status at(std::size_t i, T* out) const {
        if (out == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        if (i >= count_) return Status::NotFound;
        *out = items_[(head_ + i) % N];
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    void clear() {
        head_ = 0;
        count_ = 0;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return count_; }
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() { return N; }
    bool empty() const { return count_ == 0; }
    bool full() const { return count_ == N; }
    std::uint32_t dropped() const { return dropped_; }

private:
    T items_[N] = {};
    std::size_t head_ = 0;       // index of the oldest item
    std::size_t count_ = 0;      // how many items are held
    std::uint32_t dropped_ = 0;  // items lost to push_overwrite
};

// ---- Pool: N fixed blocks, handed out and taken back in O(1) ----------------
// A handle names a block by its index and the block's generation. Releasing a
// block bumps its generation, so an old handle to it stops working.
struct Handle {
    std::uint16_t index;
    std::uint16_t gen;   // 0 never names a live block
};

constexpr Handle kNoHandle = {0xFFFF, 0};

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class Pool {
    static_assert(N > 0 && N < 0xFFFF, "a pool holds 1 to 65534 blocks");

public:
    Pool() { reset(); }

    // Every block free again; every old handle stops working.
    void reset() {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
            next_[i] = static_cast<std::uint16_t>(i + 1);   // N marks the end
            gen_[i] = static_cast<std::uint16_t>(gen_[i] == 0xFFFF ? 1 : gen_[i] + 1);
            used_[i] = false;
        }
        free_head_ = 0;
        in_use_ = 0;
    }

    // Takes a free block, clears it to T{} and writes its handle.
    // The most recently released block is handed out first.
    Status acquire(Handle* out) {
        if (out == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        if (free_head_ == N) {
            ++failures_;
            return Status::NoSpace;
        }
        const std::uint16_t i = free_head_;
        free_head_ = next_[i];
        used_[i] = true;
        items_[i] = T{};
        ++in_use_;
        if (in_use_ > high_water_) high_water_ = in_use_;
        *out = {i, gen_[i]};
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // Gives a block back. A stale, foreign or doubled handle is refused.
    Status release(Handle h) {
        if (!valid(h)) return Status::BadArg;
        used_[h.index] = false;
        gen_[h.index] = static_cast<std::uint16_t>(gen_[h.index] == 0xFFFF ? 1 : gen_[h.index] + 1);
        next_[h.index] = free_head_;
        free_head_ = h.index;
        --in_use_;
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    bool valid(Handle h) const { return h.index < N && h.gen != 0 && used_[h.index] && gen_[h.index] == h.gen; }

    T* get(Handle h) { return valid(h) ? &items_[h.index] : nullptr; }
    const T* get(Handle h) const { return valid(h) ? &items_[h.index] : nullptr; }

    std::size_t in_use() const { return in_use_; }
    std::size_t available() const { return N - in_use_; }
    std::size_t high_water() const { return high_water_; }
    std::uint32_t failures() const { return failures_; }
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() { return N; }

private:
    T items_[N] = {};
    std::uint16_t next_[N] = {};   // free list, threaded through the indexes
    std::uint16_t gen_[N] = {};
    bool used_[N] = {};
    std::uint16_t free_head_ = 0;  // N when no block is free
    std::size_t in_use_ = 0;
    std::size_t high_water_ = 0;   // the most blocks ever in use at once
    std::uint32_t failures_ = 0;   // acquires refused because none was free
};

// ---- Packet buffers and queues that share one pool --------------------------
constexpr std::size_t kMaxPacketBytes = 128;
constexpr std::size_t kBufferCount = 24;

struct PacketBuffer {
    std::uint8_t bytes[kMaxPacketBytes];
    std::uint16_t len;
};

using BufferPool = Pool<PacketBuffer, kBufferCount>;

// A FIFO of packets. The bytes live in blocks of a shared pool; the queue
// itself holds only handles, so moving a packet never copies 128 bytes twice.
template <std::size_t Depth>
class PacketQueue {
public:
    explicit PacketQueue(BufferPool* pool) : pool_(pool) {}

    // Copies a packet in. NoSpace when the pool is used up, Full when this
    // queue is at its depth; either way nothing is queued and no block leaks.
    Status put(const std::uint8_t* bytes, std::size_t len) {
        if (pool_ == nullptr || bytes == nullptr || len == 0 || len > kMaxPacketBytes) return Status::BadArg;
        if (fifo_.full()) return Status::Full;
        Handle h;
        const Status got = pool_->acquire(&h);
        if (got != Status::Ok) return got;
        PacketBuffer* b = pool_->get(h);
        std::memcpy(b->bytes, bytes, len);
        b->len = static_cast<std::uint16_t>(len);
        fifo_.push(h);   // cannot fail: checked for room above
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // Copies the oldest packet out and frees its block. If it does not fit
    // in cap bytes it stays queued and the result is NoSpace.
    Status take(std::uint8_t* out, std::size_t cap, std::size_t* len) {
        if (pool_ == nullptr || out == nullptr || len == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        Handle h;
        const Status got = fifo_.peek(&h);
        if (got != Status::Ok) return got;
        const PacketBuffer* b = pool_->get(h);
        if (b == nullptr) return Status::NotFound;   // cannot happen while the invariant holds
        if (b->len > cap) return Status::NoSpace;
        std::memcpy(out, b->bytes, b->len);
        *len = b->len;
        fifo_.pop(&h);
        pool_->release(h);
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    // The length of the oldest packet, without taking it.
    Status front_len(std::size_t* len) const {
        if (pool_ == nullptr || len == nullptr) return Status::BadArg;
        Handle h;
        const Status got = fifo_.peek(&h);
        if (got != Status::Ok) return got;
        const PacketBuffer* b = pool_->get(h);
        if (b == nullptr) return Status::NotFound;
        *len = b->len;
        return Status::Ok;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return fifo_.size(); }
    bool empty() const { return fifo_.empty(); }
    static constexpr std::size_t depth() { return Depth; }

private:
    BufferPool* pool_;
    RingBuffer<Handle, Depth> fifo_;
};
--- hint
Keep four arrays of N: the items, `next_` (the free list), `gen_` and a `bool used_`. Plus `free_head_` (N when the list is empty), `in_use_`, `high_water_` and `failures_`. In `reset`, set `next_[i] = i + 1`, so the last block points at N, the end.
--- hint
`acquire` pops the head: `i = free_head_; free_head_ = next_[i];`. `release` pushes: `next_[i] = free_head_; free_head_ = i;`, but only after `valid(h)` said yes. Write `valid` first and use it in `release` and `get`.
--- hint
In `PacketQueue::put`, the order is: check the arguments, check `fifo_.full()`, then acquire, copy, push. In `take`, `peek` the handle, look at the block's length, copy, and only then `pop` and `release`.

+++ practice | A pool of burn plans
--- task
The guidance computer keeps up to 6 planned engine burns in a fixed table. Write the table's allocator in C style, with the free list threaded through `next`:

```cpp fragment
struct BurnTable {
    int next[6];      // the free list: the free slot after this one, or -1
    bool used[6];
    int free_head;    // the first free slot, or -1
};
```

- `void table_init(BurnTable* t)`: all six slots free, the free list in order 0, 1, ..., 5.
- `int slot_alloc(BurnTable* t)`: take the first free slot and return its number, or return -1 if none is free.
- `bool slot_free(BurnTable* t, int i)`: give slot `i` back and put it at the front of the free list. Return `false` (and change nothing) if `i` is not 0 to 5 or the slot is not in use.
--- starter
struct BurnTable {
    int next[6];
    bool used[6];
    int free_head;
};

void table_init(BurnTable* t) {
}

int slot_alloc(BurnTable* t) {
    return -1;
}

bool slot_free(BurnTable* t, int i) {
    return false;
}
--- solution
struct BurnTable {
    int next[6];
    bool used[6];
    int free_head;
};

void table_init(BurnTable* t) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
        t->next[i] = i + 1 < 6 ? i + 1 : -1;
        t->used[i] = false;
    }
    t->free_head = 0;
}

int slot_alloc(BurnTable* t) {
    if (t->free_head < 0) return -1;
    int i = t->free_head;
    t->free_head = t->next[i];
    t->used[i] = true;
    return i;
}

bool slot_free(BurnTable* t, int i) {
    if (i < 0 || i >= 6 || !t->used[i]) return false;
    t->used[i] = false;
    t->next[i] = t->free_head;
    t->free_head = i;
    return true;
}
--- hint
Taking a slot pops the head of the list; freeing pushes the slot back on the front.
--- hint
The `used` array is what lets `slot_free` refuse a slot that is already free.
--- check test | Slots come out in order, then run out
[] { BurnTable t; table_init(&t); for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) if (slot_alloc(&t) != i) return false; return slot_alloc(&t) == -1; }()
--- check test | The slot freed last is reused first
[] { BurnTable t; table_init(&t); for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) slot_alloc(&t); slot_free(&t, 2); slot_free(&t, 4); return slot_alloc(&t) == 4 && slot_alloc(&t) == 2 && slot_alloc(&t) == -1; }()
--- check test | Freeing twice, or a slot that does not exist, is refused

--- check test | A refused double free does not hand a slot out twice
