    std::fprintf(out, "--- end of hour ---\n%s\n", buf);
    std::fprintf(out, "ground: packets=%u crc_errors=%u missed=%u hk=%u acks=%u naks=%u\n",
                 static_cast<unsigned>(gs.rx().packets()), static_cast<unsigned>(gs.rx().crc_errors()),
                 static_cast<unsigned>(gs.seq().total_missed()), static_cast<unsigned>(gs.hk_count()),
                 static_cast<unsigned>(gs.acks()), static_cast<unsigned>(gs.naks()));
    std::fprintf(out, "heap allocations during the hour: %lld\n", heap_used);
}

// The whole system and the ground live in static memory, built once.
FlightSystem g_flight;
GroundStation g_ground;
Scenario g_scenario;

// Reads a scenario from standard input, flies the hour, prints the events
// and the summary. Returns 0, or 1 for a scenario that does not parse.
int mission_main() {
    static char text[8192];
    const std::size_t n = std::fread(text, 1, sizeof text - 1, stdin);
    text[n] = '\0';
    std::size_t bad = 0;
    if (parse_scenario(text, &g_scenario, &bad) != Status::Ok) {
        std::printf("scenario error on line %u\n", static_cast<unsigned>(bad));
        return 1;
    }
    const long long before = heap_allocs();
    run_hour(g_scenario, &g_flight, &g_ground, stdout);
    const long long used = heap_allocs() - before;
    print_summary(g_flight, g_ground, used, stdout);
    return 0;
}

+++ question | Why a count and not only two indexes
--- ask
The project's `RingBuffer` keeps `head_` and `count_`. A common alternative keeps only a head and a tail index. What does the count buy?
--- choice correct
With only two indexes, an empty ring and a full ring both have head equal to tail, so one slot must be left unused; the count tells the two apart and uses all N slots.
--- choice
The count makes `pop` O(1); with two indexes it would be O(N).
--- choice
The count avoids the modulo operation when the indexes wrap.
--- choice
Two indexes cannot be used with `push_overwrite`.
--- why
Both designs are O(1) and both need the wrap-around. The difference is information: two indexes that are equal could mean "nothing" or "everything". The classic fix wastes a slot; a count removes the ambiguity.

+++ question | The leak in a refused put
--- ask
Suppose `PacketQueue::put` acquired a pool block first and only then checked whether its ring of handles had room, returning `Full` without releasing the block. What happens on the spacecraft?
--- choice
Nothing: the next `put` reuses the same block.
--- choice correct
Every refused put leaks one block; after enough refusals the shared pool is empty and every queue using it fails with `NoSpace`, far from the cause.
--- choice
The ring buffer overwrites its oldest handle, so one packet is lost each time.
--- choice
The pool detects the leak because the handle's generation is wrong.
--- why
The pool only gets a block back through `release`. A block acquired and forgotten is gone for good, and because the pool is shared the symptom appears in another queue. Check first, act last; and watch that `pool.in_use()` always equals the packets queued.

+++ question | Tombstones and searches
--- ask
In the `StaticMap`, why must `erase` leave a tombstone instead of marking the slot empty?
--- choice
So that `size()` stays correct.
--- choice correct
A search stops at the first empty slot; emptying a slot in the middle of a probe run would make keys further along that run impossible to find.
--- choice
So that the erased key can be restored if the ground changes its mind.
--- choice
Because an empty slot would make `sorted_keys` list the erased key.
--- why
The map's invariant is that every slot from a key's home to its position is non-empty. A tombstone keeps that true for other keys, while still being reusable by inserts.

+++ question | What the table CRC costs
--- ask
The CRC is computed with a 256-entry table built by a `constexpr` function. Compared with the bit-at-a-time version, what does that cost and save?
--- choice
It saves nothing in time; it only makes the code shorter.
--- choice correct
512 bytes of read-only memory, no start-up time; each byte then takes one table lookup instead of eight shift-and-XOR steps. Both are O(n).
--- choice
It changes the CRC from O(n) to O(1).
--- choice
It uses 512 bytes of heap at start-up, which is allowed because start-up is before the rule applies.
--- why
The compiler computes the table, so it lives in the program image and costs nothing when the program starts. The work per byte drops by about a factor of eight, but it is still linear in the message length.

+++ question | The order of the decoder's checks
--- ask
`decode_packet` reports `BadLength` for an impossible length field before it reports `TooShort` for missing bytes. Why does the stream decoder need that order?
--- choice
`BadLength` is more serious, so it should be reported first.
--- choice
The CRC check needs to come last, and `BadLength` happens to be next to it.
--- choice correct
`TooShort` makes the stream decoder wait for more bytes; if a damaged length could produce `TooShort` first, the decoder could wait on garbage instead of skipping it.
--- choice
Checking the length first avoids a division by zero.
--- why
The stream decoder treats `TooShort` as "the rest has not arrived yet" and everything else as "garbage: drop a byte and resynchronise". Reporting nonsense lengths as `BadLength` keeps a damaged header from being mistaken for a packet still arriving.

+++ question | Why a failed build must not use a sequence count
--- ask
In `PacketEncoder::build`, the APID's sequence count only advances when the packet is built. What goes wrong if a failed build (say, `NoSpace`) advanced it too?
--- choice correct
The ground's sequence tracker sees a gap and reports a lost packet that was never sent.
--- choice
The next packet would reuse the same count, and the ground would report a duplicate.
--- choice
The CRC of the next packet would be wrong.
--- choice
Nothing, because the count wraps at 16384 anyway.
--- why
Gaps in the counts are how the ground detects lost packets. A count used by nothing makes a phantom gap, and people start looking for a radio problem that does not exist.

+++ question | A persistence count of 5
--- ask
A limit monitor has a set count of 5 and a clear count of 10, and samples arrive at 10 Hz after the filters. The bus voltage suddenly drops into red and stays there. Ignoring the filters' lag, how many samples after the drop is the state first reported red, and what is the price of that delay?
--- choice
On the first sample; persistence only affects clearing.
--- choice correct
On the 5th red sample, about 0.5 s later: the delay buys immunity to noise that crosses the limit for fewer than 5 samples in a row.
--- choice
On the 10th sample, because red needs both counts.
--- choice
On the 6th sample, because the counter is compared before it is incremented.
--- why
The run counter is bumped and then compared, so the change happens on the set_count-th sample. Persistence trades a known, small delay for far fewer false alarms; the filters add their own lag on top.

+++ question | Who pays when a task overruns
--- ask
In the cyclic executive, the 10 Hz SENSE task (first in its frame) takes 70 ms more than its budget in a frame that also holds HK (period 10). What happens?
--- choice
SENSE is stopped when it reaches its budget.
--- choice
The next frame starts 70 ms late, and the schedule slips permanently.
--- choice correct
Tasks later in the frame whose budgets no longer fit are skipped this frame and counted; with rate-monotonic order these are the low-rate tasks such as HK, and FDIR later sees the budget overrun in the counters.
--- choice
The scheduler reorders the frame so HK runs first next time.
--- why
Without preemption nothing can stop SENSE. The admission check protects the end of the frame by skipping tasks whose whole budget no longer fits, and rate-monotonic order means the least frequent tasks are the ones squeezed.

+++ question | Exactly the right number of argument bytes
--- ask
The command handler rejects a SET_MODE command that carries 2 argument bytes instead of 1 with `BAD_ARGS`, even though the first byte is a valid mode. Why is that the right design?
--- choice
Extra bytes waste uplink bandwidth.
--- choice correct
Extra bytes mean the ground and the flight software disagree about the command's format; running it would read the arguments with the wrong layout, so the disagreement must be made visible.
--- choice
The CRC would not cover the extra byte.
--- choice
The `ByteReader` cannot read a partial buffer.
--- why
The command database on the ground and the table on board must match. A length mismatch is the cheapest possible detector of a mismatched version, and refusing the command costs nothing but a NAK the operators will notice.

+++ question | Why FDIR has budgets
--- ask
A fault rule says "Recover twice, then Isolate". What problem do the budget and the second response solve?
--- choice
They make the response faster.
--- choice
They let the ground change the response without a command.
--- choice correct
Without a budget, a recovery that does not really fix the cause would repeat forever; the budget turns "keep trying" into "try twice, then escalate".
--- choice
They prevent the fault from being latched twice.
--- why
Recovery loops are a classic flight software failure: the same reset repeated thousands of times while the real problem is never escalated. A budget bounds the attempts, and a cleared latch restores it when the ground has looked.

+++ question | Heap allocations during the hour
--- ask
The mission summary prints the number of heap allocations made during the simulated hour, and it must be 0. Which of these, added to a task, would break it?
--- choice
A local `std::uint8_t buf[128];` in the task function.
--- choice
A `static` `RingBuffer<Event, 64>` inside the task function.
--- choice correct
A `std::string` built with `+=` to format an event before logging it.
--- choice
Calling `std::snprintf` into a fixed char array.
--- why
A growing `std::string` goes through `operator new`, which the heap watch counts. Local arrays live on the stack, statics are placed before the program runs, and `snprintf` writes into memory the caller provides.

+++ question | What the ground's missed count means
--- ask
At the end of the lesson's hour, the ground reported `crc_errors=3 missed=3`: three downlinked packets were corrupted on purpose. Why is the missed count also 3?
--- answer
Each corrupted packet was dropped by the decoder, so its sequence count never reached the tracker, and the next good packet on that APID showed a gap of one.
each corrupted packet left a gap of one in its APID's sequence counts
each dropped packet made a gap of one
--- why
The two counters see the same loss from two sides: the stream decoder counts the damaged packets it rejected, and the sequence tracker counts the numbers that never arrived. When they agree, the ground knows the loss was all corruption, not packets that were never sent.
